\begin{abstract}
Let $f:\N\to\{z\in\C:|z|\leq1\}$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$\alpha$ has a rational approximation $a/q$ with
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq 1/(qx)$ and $q\leq x/((\log x)^2(\log\log x)^3)$. We prove that
\[
 \left|\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)\e(n\alpha)\right|
 \leq \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q} +O\left(\frac{x}{\log x}\right).
\]
whereas complete multiplicativity improves $4/\sqrt6$ to $1$.
Both constants are optimal. In particular, this confirms a \rev{folklore} conjecture on exponential sums with multiplicative coefficients motivated
by the work of Montgomery and Vaughan (1977).
\rev{We also obtain logarithmically weighted estimates and give counterexamples to related conjectures.}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Let $\U:=\{z\in\C:|z|\leq1\}$ and
$\e(t):=\exp(2\pi i t)$. For a multiplicative function
$f:\N\to\U$, write
$S_f(x,\alpha):=\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)\e(n\alpha)$.
We are interested in how large this sum can be when
$\alpha$ is close to a rational number.

There are two natural reasons why such sums can be large.
If $f$ is a primitive Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and
$\alpha=a/q$, the Gauss sum gives a contribution of size
$x/\sqrt q$. On the other hand, by choosing the values of
$f(p)$ for primes $p$ comparable with $x$, one can obtain
a contribution of size $x/\log x$. These two examples suggest
that the correct upper bound should contain both terms.

This leads to the following folklore conjecture.

\begin{conjecture}\label{conj:main}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative,
and suppose that $|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, where
$(a,q)=1$ and $1\leq q\leq x/(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conjecture}
 |S_f(x,\alpha)|
 \ll_\varepsilon
 \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
\end{conjecture}

The study of exponential sums with multiplicative
coefficients goes back to Daboussi and Delange
\cite{DaboussiDelange1974,DaboussiDelange1982},
who established cancellation for irrational additive
phases. Montgomery and Vaughan
\cite{MontgomeryVaughan1977} later obtained the
quantitative estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:MV-intro}
 |S_f(x,a/q)|
 \ll \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}
\end{equation}
for $q\leq x/((\log x)^2(\log\log x)^3)$.
The difference between $\phi(q)$ and $q$ matters here,
since $q/\phi(q)$ can be arbitrarily large.

Further progress was made by de la Bret\`eche and
Granville \cite{BretecheGranville2022}, who obtained
the expected $x/\sqrt q$ bound for completely
multiplicative functions when
$q\leq(\log x)^{2-\delta}$, for any fixed $\delta>0$.
Granville and Lamzouri \cite{GranvilleLamzouri2026}
extended the discussion to general multiplicative
functions and showed that the main difficulty lies
in the transition range $q=(\log x)^{2+o(1)}$.
Outside this range, the conjecture follows from
the existing estimates.

Our first result proves the conjecture throughout the
range covered by Montgomery and Vaughan. We also
determine the best possible leading constants.
Write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QMV}
 Q_{\rm MV}(x):=
 \frac{x}{(\log x)^2(\log\log x)^3}.
\end{equation}

\begin{thm}[Sharp exponential-sum bounds]\label{thm:main}
Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, where $(a,q)=1$ and
$1\leq q\leq Q_{\rm MV}(x)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-expanded}
 |S_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}
 +O\left(\frac{x}{\log x}\right).
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-main}
 |S_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq
 (1+o(1))\frac{x}{\sqrt q}
 +O\left(\frac{x}{\log x}\right).
\end{equation}
Both leading constants are best possible, and the
estimates are uniform in $f,a,q$, and $\alpha$.
In particular, Conjecture~\ref{conj:main} holds
for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
\end{thm}

\begin{rem}
\rev{Independently,} Robles \cite{Robles2026} proved the folklore
conjecture for all $1$-bounded multiplicative functions,
\rev{in the wider range} $q\leq x/(\log x)^2$ \rev{under the weaker approximation condition}
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq q^{-2}$. His result gives the conjectured
upper bound, but does not determine the sharp leading
constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$ \rev{as in our}
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
\end{rem}

\rev{The difference between these constants comes from the local factors.}
For general multiplicative functions, the constant
$4/\sqrt6$ comes from the local contributions at
the primes $2$ and $3$. Complete multiplicativity
forces additional cancellation in these local factors,
which reduces the constant to $1$.

When $q=o((\log x)^2)$, the term $x/\log x$ is
smaller than $x/\sqrt q$ and can be absorbed into
the error in the leading coefficient. We therefore
obtain the following consequence.

\begin{cor}\label{cor:sharp-range}
\rev{Suppose that} $q=o((\log x)^2)$ \rev{and that the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} hold. Then}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subcritical-general}
 |S_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
For completely multiplicative $f$, the constant
$4/\sqrt6$ can be replaced by $1$.
Both constants are optimal, and neither estimate
can be extended uniformly to $q\asymp(\log x)^2$
with the same leading constant.
\end{cor}

We also consider the logarithmically weighted sum
$\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)\e(n\alpha)/n$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, together with partial
summation, gives the following bounds.
\rev{These logarithmic estimates are also established directly in}
\cite{GouLogarithmic2026},
using a two-prime Ramar\'e identity.

\begin{cor}[Logarithmic exponential sums]
\label{cor:logarithmic}
Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, where $(a,q)=1$ and
$1\leq q\leq x$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:logarithmic-corollary}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}n\e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \ll \log q+\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
In particular, conjecture~(1.5) of
\cite{GranvilleLamzouri2026} holds.

Moreover, if
$q=o((\log x/\log\log x)^2)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-sharp-log}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}n\e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leq
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, the stronger
estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-sharp-log}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}n\e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leq
 (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
\end{equation}
holds in the same range.

The leading constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$ are
best possible for multiplicative and completely
multiplicative functions, respectively.
All estimates are uniform in $f,a,q$, and $\alpha$.
\end{cor}

It is natural to ask whether the sharp constants
remain valid in larger ranges, or whether similar
estimates hold for sums over smooth numbers.
Some of these stronger statements turn out to be
false. We give three counterexamples to conjectures
(1.3), (1.4), and (1.6) of
\cite{GranvilleLamzouri2026}.

As usual, $P^+(n)$ denotes the largest prime factor
of $n$, and $\Psi(x,y)$ denotes the number of integers
$n\leq x$ for which $P^+(n)\leq y$.

\begin{prop}[Three counterexamples]\label{prop:counterexamples}
The following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item
There are $1$-bounded multiplicative functions $f_j$
and parameters $q_j,x_j\to\infty$, with
$q_j\leq(\log x_j)^2$, such that
\[
 |S_{f_j}(x_j,1/q_j)|
 =
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{x_j}{\sqrt{q_j}}.
\]
Thus the leading constant $1$ in conjecture~(1.3)
is false for general multiplicative functions.

\item
There are squarefree integers $q_j\to\infty$,
real numbers $x_j\geq y_j\geq q_j^2$ tending to
infinity, reduced numerators $a_j$, and periodic
unimodular multiplicative functions $f_j$ such that
\[
 \frac{
 \left|
 \sum_{\substack{n\leq x_j\\P^+(n)\leq y_j}}
 f_j(n)\e(a_jn/q_j)
 \right|
 }{
 \Psi(x_j,y_j)/\sqrt{q_j}
 +\sqrt{x_jy_j}/\log x_j
 }
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Hence conjecture~(1.4) fails in order of magnitude.

\item
For $f\equiv1$ and
$q=\lfloor(\log x/\log\log x)^2\rfloor$, we have
\[
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leq x}\frac{\e(n/q)}n
 \right|
 =(2+o(1))\log\log x.
\]
This exceeds the proposed upper bound with leading
constant $4/\sqrt6$ in conjecture~(1.6).
Thus that conjecture fails at its stated endpoint,
even for completely multiplicative functions.

\end{enumerate}
\end{prop}

These examples illustrate three different
obstructions. The first comes from the local
behavior of a multiplicative function at small
primes. The second shows that smooth-number sums
can contain additional Euler factors whose size
grows with $q$. The third shows why the $\log q$
term in \eqref{eq:logarithmic-corollary} cannot
always be removed.

\subsection{Some background}

A central idea in the study of multiplicative
functions is that a large mean often comes from
a function which resembles $\chi(n)n^{it}$, where
$\chi$ is a Dirichlet character and $t$ is real.
This is the starting point of the pretentious
approach developed by Granville and Soundararajan
\cite{GranvilleSoundararajan2007}.
Related results were obtained by Goldmakher
\cite{Goldmakher2012} and by Bober, Goldmakher,
Granville and Koukoulopoulos
\cite{BoberGoldmakherGranvilleKoukoulopoulos2018}.

An important tool for us is the pretentious
large sieve of Granville, Harper and Soundararajan
\cite{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019}.
Roughly speaking, it says that the character
sums associated with a bounded multiplicative
function cannot be large for too many
Dirichlet characters at once. In the range
we need, it allows us to remove all but one
possible exceptional character.

Another ingredient comes from the theory of
smooth numbers. Exponential sums over smooth
numbers have been studied by de la Bret\`eche
\cite{Breteche1998}, Maier \cite{Maier2006},
and de la Bret\`eche and Tenenbaum
\cite{BretecheTenenbaum2007}.
Their work is closely related to the distribution
of smooth numbers in arithmetic progressions,
studied by Fouvry and Tenenbaum
\cite{FouvryTenenbaum1991}, Granville
\cite{Granville1993}, and Harper
\cite{Harper2012}. Further estimates were
obtained by Harper \cite{Harper2016}.

Granville and Lamzouri
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}
obtained an upper bound for exponential sums
over smooth numbers. Their estimate contains
an additional factor $2^{\omega(q)/2}$ in the
smooth contribution\rev{, where $\omega(q)$ denotes the number of distinct prime factors of $q$}. This factor is harmless
in some ranges, but it cannot be absorbed
uniformly near $q=(\log x)^2$.

Our approach is to apply Ramar\'e's identity
before expanding into Dirichlet characters.
This keeps the multiplicative structure of
the sum and allows us to use Shiu's theorem
together with the pretentious large sieve
without introducing that extra factor.

\subsection{Outline of the proof}

\rev{We briefly describe the proof.}

We first reduce a general multiplicative function
to one which is completely multiplicative at
primes not dividing $q$. The important point is
that we keep all the original values at prime
powers dividing $q$. A direct reduction to a
completely multiplicative function could change
the denominator of the rational phase, which
would make the resulting estimate weaker.

Next, we separate the integers according to
whether they have a prime factor greater than
$x/q$. Such integers \rev{can be written uniquely as}
$n=pm$, where $p>x/q$ is prime and $m<q$.
We group the primes according to the length
of the inner sum over $m$. Brun--Titchmarsh
and a simple second-moment argument then show
that their total contribution is $O(x/\log x)$.
For the shortest sums, we use the exact
structure of Ramanujan sums to avoid a loss
depending on $q/\phi(q)$.

It remains to treat integers whose prime factors
are all at most $x/q$. Here we use Ramar\'e's
identity to extract one prime factor larger than
$(\log x)^{10}$. The usual Ramar\'e weight
is not multiplicative, so we write it as an
integral instead. This introduces the weight
$z^{\omega_T(n)}$, where $\omega_T(n)$ counts
the distinct prime factors of $n$ exceeding
$T=(\log x)^{10}$.

The advantage is that, for each fixed $z$,
this weight is multiplicative and non-negative.
We can therefore apply Shiu's theorem to
estimate the resulting weighted sums in
arithmetic progressions.

We then expand the sums into Dirichlet
characters modulo $q$. The pretentious
large sieve shows that all but at most one
character make a negligible contribution.
The remaining character is controlled
using Gauss sums and Shiu's theorem.
Finally, the integration over $z$ allows
us to sum over all prime intervals without
losing an extra factor of $\log\log x$.
This gives the required bound
$S_f(x,\alpha)\ll x/\log x+x/\sqrt q$.

To obtain the sharp constants, we go a step
further. We show that, up to a smaller error,
the original exponential sum is governed by
a single Dirichlet character. We then write
each integer as $n=dm$, where every prime
factor of $d$ divides $q$ and $(m,q)=1$.
This separates the ordinary character sum
from a factor involving Gauss sums.

The size of this factor determines the leading
constant. For general multiplicative functions,
its absolute norm is bounded by
$(4/\sqrt6)\sqrt q$. For completely
multiplicative functions, the local Euler
factors have additional cancellation, giving
the smaller bound $\sqrt q$. These are exactly
the two constants in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

Sections~\ref{sec:prelim}--\ref{sec:reduction}
give the preliminary reductions, and
Section~\ref{sec:large-prime} treats the
large-prime contribution.
Sections~\ref{sec:ramare}--\ref{sec:summing}
contain the Ramar\'e and \rev{Fourier-analytic} arguments.
Section~\ref{sec:completion} proves the
order-of-magnitude estimate, while
Section~\ref{sec:sharp-general} gives
the sharp constants. The logarithmic
applications and counterexamples are
proved in Sections~\ref{sec:logarithmic}
and~\ref{sec:counterexamples}.

\section{Notation and preliminary reductions}\label{sec:prelim}

The largest prime factor of $n$ is denoted by $P^{+}(n)$, with $P^{+}(1)=1$, and
$\Psi(X,Y):=\#\{n\leq X:P^{+}(n)\leq Y\}$. Throughout the proof,
$L=\log x$ and
\[
 c_q(h):=\sum_{r\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}\e(hr/q)
\]
is the Ramanujan sum. \rev{Unless otherwise stated, implied constants are absolute;
dependence on fixed parameters is indicated explicitly.} Dirichlet
characters are understood modulo the current modulus and are extended by
zero away from its unit group.

For a multiplicative function $g$ with Dirichlet series
$G(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}g(n)n^{-s}$, define its generalized von Mangoldt
coefficients by
$-G'(s)/G(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}\Lambda_g(n)n^{-s}$. Following
\cite{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019}, we write $g\in\mathcal C(1)$
when $|\Lambda_g(n)|\leq\Lambda(n)$ for every $n$, where $\Lambda$ is
the ordinary von Mangoldt function.

\rev{We shall sometimes replace the rational phase $a/q$ by a nearby real phase. The following elementary estimate is enough.}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:phase}
If $|\alpha-a/q|\leq 1/(qX)$ and $|f(n)|\leq1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase}
 |S_f(X,\alpha)-S_f(X,a/q)|\ll \frac{X}{q}.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Using $|\e(t)-1|\ll|t|$, the left-hand side is at most
$|\alpha-a/q|\sum_{n\leq X}n\ll X/q$.
\end{proof}

We first dispose of the range in which the Montgomery--Vaughan theorem is already stronger than required.

\begin{prop}\label{prop:large-q}
Suppose that $(a,q)=1$, $L^{5/2}\leq q\leq Q_{\rm MV}(x)$, and
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$. Then
$S_f(x,\alpha)\ll x/L$.
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
\rev{For these values of $q$,} \cite[Theorem~1]{MontgomeryVaughan1977} gives \eqref{eq:MV-intro}. The standard estimate $q/\phi(q)\ll\log\log(3q)$ yields
$x/\sqrt{\phi(q)}\ll x\sqrt{\log\log(3q)/q}=o(x/L)$ when $q\geq L^{5/2}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:phase} contributes $O(x/q)=o(x/L)$.
\end{proof}

It remains to treat $q\leq L^3$. \rev{This range overlaps with that of}
Proposition~\ref{prop:large-q}\rev{, so together they cover all admissible denominators.}

\section{Reduction to complete multiplicativity away from \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}}\label{sec:reduction}

A standard passage from multiplicative to completely multiplicative functions may lower the denominator from $q$ to $q/(q,d)$ inside a convolution. The following variant avoids this loss.

For fixed $q$, define a multiplicative function $F_q$ on prime powers by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Fq}
 F_q(p^k):=\begin{cases}f(p^k),&p\mid q,\\ f(p)^k,&p\nmid q.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Thus $F_q$ is completely multiplicative at every prime not dividing $q$, while the full local data of $f$ are retained at the primes dividing $q$.

\begin{lem}\label{lem:conv}
There is a multiplicative function $h$ such that $f=h*F_q$, with $h(p^k)=0$ for $p\mid q$, $h(p)=0$ for $p\nmid q$, and
$h(p^k)=f(p^k)-f(p)f(p^{k-1})$ for $p\nmid q$ and $k\geq2$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:h-sums}
 \sum_{d\geq1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}<\infty,
 \qquad
 \sum_{d\geq1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d^{1-\delta}}<\infty
 \quad(0<\delta<1/2).
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Define $h$ multiplicatively by the identity of formal Euler factors
\[
 \sum_{k\geq0}\frac{f(p^k)}{p^{ks}}
 =\left(\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{h(p^k)}{p^{ks}}\right)
  \left(\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{F_q(p^k)}{p^{ks}}\right).
\]
If $p\mid q$, the two factors involving $f$ and $F_q$ are identical, whence $h(p^k)=0$ for every $k\geq1$. Suppose that $p\nmid q$. Since $F_q(p^k)=f(p)^k$, comparison of the coefficient of $p^{-s}$ gives $h(p)=0$. For $k\geq2$, the coefficient identity reads
$f(p^k)=h(p^k)+f(p)h(p^{k-1})+\cdots+f(p)^k$. Using the same identity at level $k-1$ and multiplying it by $f(p)$, all terms except the first cancel, and therefore
$h(p^k)=f(p^k)-f(p)f(p^{k-1})$.

It follows that $|h(p^k)|\leq2$, and that every integer in the support of $h$, apart from $1$, is powerful and coprime to $q$. Hence
\[
 \sum_{d\geq1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}
 \leq\prod_{p\nmid q}\left(1+2\sum_{k\geq2}\frac1{p^k}\right)
 \leq\prod_p\left(1+\frac{2}{p(p-1)}\right)<\infty.
\]
More generally, if $0<\delta<1/2$, then
$\sum_{k\geq2}p^{-k(1-\delta)}\ll p^{-2(1-\delta)}$, and the corresponding Euler product converges because $2(1-\delta)>1$. This proves both assertions in \eqref{eq:h-sums}.
\end{proof}

\begin{prop}\label{prop:reduction}
Suppose that, whenever $X$ is large, $q\leq8(\log X)^3$, and
$F:\N\to\U$ is multiplicative and completely multiplicative at every
prime $p\nmid q$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-goal}
 S_F(X,\theta)\ll \frac{X}{\log X}+\frac{X}{\sqrt q}
\end{equation}
for $|\theta-b/q|\leq1/(qX)$ and $(b,q)=1$. Then the same estimate
holds, under the same approximation hypothesis, for every multiplicative
$f:\N\to\U$ whenever $q\leq(\log x)^3$.
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Expanding the convolution $f=h*F_q$ and changing the order of summation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conv-sum}
 S_f(x,\alpha)=\sum_{\substack{d\leq x\\(d,q)=1}}h(d)S_{F_q}(x/d,d\alpha).
\end{equation}
The restriction $(d,q)=1$ \rev{follows from} Lemma~\ref{lem:conv}.
Since $(d,q)=1$, \rev{$ad$ is also coprime to $q$}, and
\[
 d\alpha=\frac{ad}{q}+d(\alpha-a/q),
 \qquad |d(\alpha-a/q)|\leq\frac{d}{qx}=\frac1{q(x/d)}.
\]
Thus every inner sum in \eqref{eq:conv-sum} has a rational approximation with the same denominator $q$. This is the point of the definition \eqref{eq:Fq}.

We split the $d$-sum at $\sqrt x$. If $d\leq\sqrt x$, then
$x/d\geq\sqrt x$ and $\log x\leq2\log(x/d)$. Consequently
$q\leq(\log x)^3\leq8(\log(x/d))^3$, so \eqref{eq:local-goal}
applies. Since $\log(x/d)\asymp\log x$ in this range,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{d\leq\sqrt x}|h(d)|\left(\frac{x/d}{\log(x/d)}+\frac{x/d}{\sqrt q}\right)
 &\ll \left(\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}\right)
       \sum_{d\geq1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}\\
 &\ll \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{align*}
For $d>\sqrt x$ we use $|S_{F_q}(x/d,d\alpha)|\leq x/d$.
Taking $\delta=1/4$ in \eqref{eq:h-sums},
\[
 x\sum_{d>\sqrt x}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}
 \leq x^{7/8}\sum_{d\geq1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d^{3/4}}
 \ll x^{7/8}=o(x/\log x).
\]
Combining the two ranges proves the proposition.
\end{proof}

\rev{Until Section~\ref{sec:completion}, we use $F$ for a $1$-bounded multiplicative function
that is completely multiplicative at every prime not dividing $q$.}
\rev{We assume} $(a,q)=1$ and $q\leq8L^3$, and prove
\eqref{eq:local-goal} uniformly in this range.

\section{The contribution of a large prime factor}\label{sec:large-prime}

Since $q\leq8L^3$, we have $x/q>\sqrt x$ for large $x$.
Thus every $n\leq x$ with $P^{+}(n)>x/q$ has a unique representation
$n=pm$, where $p>x/q$ is prime and $m<q$.
\rev{The key parameter is the length $\lfloor x/p\rfloor$ of the inner sum.}
We group primes for which this length is fixed. Additive Parseval controls the
longer resulting sums, whereas the exact support of the Ramanujan kernel
controls the shortest ones without a loss depending on $q/\phi(q)$.

\begin{prop}\label{prop:large-prime}
Uniformly for $q\leq8L^3$ and $(a,q)=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-prime}
 \sum_{\substack{n\leq x\\P^{+}(n)>x/q}}F(n)\e(an/q)\ll \frac{x}{\log x}.
\end{equation}
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Let $n\leq x$ satisfy $P^{+}(n)>x/q$. Since $x/q>\sqrt x$, the largest prime factor of $n$ occurs to the first power and is the unique prime factor of $n$ exceeding $x/q$. Thus $n=pm$ uniquely, where $p>x/q$ is prime and $m<x/p<q$. In particular $p\nmid m$, so ordinary multiplicativity gives $F(pm)=F(p)F(m)$.

For $1\leq k<q$, put $I_k=(x/(k+1),x/k]$ and
$A_k(b):=\sum_{m\leq k}F(m)\e(abm/q)$. The condition $p\in I_k$ is equivalent to $\lfloor x/p\rfloor=k$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-prime-decomp}
 \sum_{\substack{n\leq x\\P^{+}(n)>x/q}}F(n)\e(an/q)
 =\sum_{k<q}\sum_{p\in I_k}F(p)A_k(p).
\end{equation}
The length of $I_k$ is
$|I_k|=x/(k(k+1))\asymp x/k^2$. Since $k<q\leq8L^3$, we have
$|I_k|/q\geq x/q^3=x^{1-o(1)}$. The short-interval
Brun--Titchmarsh inequality bounds the primes in an interval of length
$H>q$ and a reduced class by
$\ll H/\{\phi(q)\log(H/q)\}$. \rev{Applying this to} $I_k$ \rev{as in}
\cite[(3.20)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026} \rev{gives}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BT}
 \#\{p\in I_k:p\equiv b\pmod q\}
 \ll \frac{x}{\phi(q)k^2\log x}
\end{equation}
for every reduced residue class $b\pmod q$, uniformly in $k<q$. Here the logarithm in Brun--Titchmarsh is $\log(|I_k|/q)\asymp\log x$.

Define
$\mathcal E_q(k):=\phi(q)^{-1}\sum_{b\bmod q,(b,q)=1}|A_k(b)|^2$. Grouping the primes in the inner sum of \eqref{eq:large-prime-decomp} by residue class, and then using \eqref{eq:BT}, gives
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{p\in I_k}F(p)A_k(p)\right|
 &\leq\sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}|A_k(b)|
       \#\{p\in I_k:p\equiv b\pmod q\}\\
 &\ll \frac{x}{\phi(q)k^2\log x}
       \sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}|A_k(b)|\\
 &\leq \frac{x}{k^2\log x}\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}.
\end{align*}
Thus each $k$-block is bounded by $x\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}/(k^2\log x)$.

We estimate $\mathcal E_q(k)$ in two different ways. Enlarging the average from the reduced residue classes to all additive frequencies and applying Parseval gives
\[
 \mathcal E_q(k)
 \leq\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{b\bmod q}|A_k(b)|^2
 =\frac q{\phi(q)}\sum_{m\leq k}|F(m)|^2
 \leq\frac q{\phi(q)}k.
\]
For small $k$ one can do better. Expanding the square over reduced residue classes yields the exact identity
\[
 \mathcal E_q(k)=\frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{m,n\leq k}F(m)\ov{F(n)}c_q(m-n).
\]
The diagonal contributes at most $k$, while for each $1\leq h<k$ there are at most $k$ pairs with $m-n=h$ and at most $k$ with $n-m=h$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy-ramanujan}
 \mathcal E_q(k)\leq k+2k\sum_{1\leq h<k}\frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}.
\end{equation}
The prime-power formula for Ramanujan sums implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ram-support}
 \frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}=
 \begin{cases}
  \phi((u,\rad(q)))/\phi(\rad(q)),&h=\frac{q}{\rad(q)}u,\\
  0,&\frac{q}{\rad(q)}\nmid h.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $p^a\Vert q$ the local factor vanishes unless $p^{a-1}\mid h$; after writing $h=(q/\rad(q))u$, it is $1$ if $p\mid u$ and $1/(p-1)$ otherwise. Therefore,
\[
 \sum_{1\leq h<k}\frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}
 \leq\frac1{\phi(\rad(q))}\sum_{u\leq k\rad(q)/q}\phi((u,\rad(q)))
 \leq\frac{k^2}{\phi(\rad(q))}.
\]
If $k\leq(q/\phi(q))^2$, then
\[
 \frac{k^2}{\phi(\rad(q))}\leq\frac{(q/\phi(q))^4}{\phi(\rad(q))}
 =\prod_{p\mid q}\frac{p^4}{(p-1)^5}\leq\frac{81}{2}.
\]
\rev{The last inequality holds because each local factor is less than $1$ for $p\geq5$, while the factors at $2$ and $3$ have product $81/2$.} Substitution in \eqref{eq:energy-ramanujan} gives
$\mathcal E_q(k)\leq82k$ for $k\leq(q/\phi(q))^2$.

We now sum the blocks. For $k\leq(q/\phi(q))^2$ use the short estimate, and for larger $k$ use Parseval:
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k<q}\frac{\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}}{k^2}
 &\ll\sum_{k\leq(q/\phi(q))^2}k^{-3/2}
   +\sqrt{q/\phi(q)}\sum_{k>(q/\phi(q))^2}k^{-3/2}\\
 &\ll1.
\end{align*}
Summing the preceding block estimate over $k<q$ proves \eqref{eq:large-prime}.
\end{proof}


\section{Ramar\'e's identity for the smooth-number contribution}
\label{sec:ramare}

Put $L=\log x$, $T=L^{10}$ and $y=x/q$. Recall that $q\leq8L^3$ and
that $F$ is completely multiplicative at every prime $p\nmid q$.
We must estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:core-def}
 C(x):=\sum_{\substack{n\leq x\\ P^+(n)\leq y}}F(n)\e(an/q).
\end{equation}
Rather than partitioning according to the largest prime factor, we
apply a Ramar\'e identity \cite[\S17.3]{Ramare2009} to
\emph{all} primes above $T$. \rev{The averaging in this identity is essential to avoid losing a factor of $\log\log x$.}

For $n\geq1$, put
\[
 \omega_T(n):=\#\{p>T:p\mid n\},\qquad
 w_z(n):=z^{\omega_T(n)}\quad(0\leq z\leq1),
\]
with $0^0=1$. The function $w_z$ is non-negative and multiplicative;
$w_z(p^k)=1$ for $p\leq T$ and $w_z(p^k)=z$ for $p>T$.
For every $n$ with $\omega_T(n)\geq1$ in which all primes $p>T$
occur to the first power, the identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-integral}
 1=\sum_{\substack{p\mid n\\p>T}}
   \frac1{\omega_T(n)}
 =\sum_{\substack{p\mid n\\p>T}}
   \int_0^1 w_z(n/p)\,\d z
\end{equation}
follows from $\int_0^1z^k\,\d z=1/(k+1)$.
The excluded integers contribute at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-exceptions}
 \Psi(x,T)+\sum_{p>T}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^2}\right\rfloor
 \ll \Psi(x,T)+\frac{x}{T}=o(x/L).
\end{equation}
Indeed, Rankin's trick with exponent $99/100$ gives
$\Psi(x,T)\leq x^{99/100+o(1)}$.
Since $T>q$, whenever $T<p\leq y$ and $m\leq x/p$,
we have $m<x/T<y$; hence $P^+(m)<y$ is automatic.
\rev{The terms with $p\mid m$ contribute at most}
$O(x/T)$\rev{, so multiplicativity gives}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-decomp}
 C(x)=\int_0^1\sum_{T<p\leq y}F(p)
  \sum_{m\leq x/p}F(m)w_z(m)\e(apm/q)\,\d z
  +O\left(\Psi(x,T)+\frac{x}{T}\right).
\end{equation}

Define the prime blocks by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-blocks}
 t_0=T,\qquad t_{j+1}=t_j+t_j^{2/3},\qquad
 \Delta_j=t_j^{2/3},\qquad M_j=x/t_j,
\end{equation}
and let $J$ be the least integer for which $t_J\geq y$.
For $0\leq j<J$, define on $(\Z/q\Z)^\times$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Aj}
 A_{j,z}(r):=\sum_{m\leq M_j}F(m)w_z(m)\e(amr/q).
\end{equation}
If $t_j<p\leq t_{j+1}$, replacing $x/p$ by $M_j$ introduces
an error bounded by $1+x\Delta_j/t_j^2$, uniformly in $z$.
Consequently the total freezing error is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-freezing}
 \ll x\sum_{j<J}\frac{\Delta_j^2}{t_j^2}+\pi(y)
 \ll xT^{-1/3}+\frac{y}{\log y}.
\end{equation}
By the short-interval Brun--Titchmarsh inequality, uniformly for
$(r,q)=1$,
\[
 \#\{t_j<p\leq\min(t_{j+1},y):p\equiv r\pmod q\}
 \ll\frac{\Delta_j}{\phi(q)\log t_j},
\]
since $\log(\Delta_j/q)\gg\log t_j$.
Combining this with \eqref{eq:ramare-decomp} and
\eqref{eq:ramare-freezing} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-master}
 |C(x)|\ll
 \int_0^1\sum_{j<J}\frac{\Delta_j}{\phi(q)\log t_j}
 \sum_{r\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}|A_{j,z}(r)|\,\d z
 +\Psi(x,T)+xT^{-1/3}+\frac{y}{\log y}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Shiu's theorem for the Ramar\'e weights}

For $u\geq1$ set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-def}
 \rho_z(u):=\min\left\{1,
 \left(\frac{\log(2T)}{\log(2u)}\right)^{1-z}\right\}
 \qquad (0\leq z\leq1).
\end{equation}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:shiu-weight}
Uniformly for $0\leq z\leq1$ and $u\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shiu-total}
 \sum_{m\leq u}w_z(m)\ll u\rho_z(u).
\end{equation}
If $u\geq q^4$, then uniformly for every $b\pmod q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shiu-progression}
 \sum_{\substack{m\leq u\\m\equiv b\pmod q}}w_z(m)
 \ll\frac uq\rho_z(u).
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Shiu's Brun--Titchmarsh theorem for non-negative multiplicative
functions \cite{Shiu1980}, combined with Mertens' estimate, gives
\[
 \sum_{m\leq u}w_z(m)
 \ll\frac{u}{\log(2u)}
   \exp\left(\sum_{p\leq u}\frac{w_z(p)}p\right)
 \ll u\rho_z(u).
\]
For small $u\ll T$ the same assertion follows trivially, since
$w_z(m)\leq1$ and $\rho_z(u)\asymp1$.
For the progression estimate, let $d=(b,q)$, $q_1=q/d$ and $u_1=u/d$.
Dividing the congruence by $d$ gives a reduced class modulo $q_1$.
Every prime dividing $d$ is below $T$, so $w_z(dm)=w_z(m)$.
Moreover $u\geq q^4$ ensures $q_1\leq u_1^{1/4}$.
Shiu's theorem, with the prime factors of $q_1$ omitted from its
Euler product, gives
\[
 \sum_{\substack{m\leq u_1\\m\equiv b/d\pmod{q_1}}}w_z(m)
 \ll\frac{u_1}{\phi(q_1)}\rho_z(u_1)
       \prod_{p\mid q_1}\left(1-\frac1p\right).
\]
Here $w_z(p)=1$ for $p\mid q_1$; the final product cancels
$q_1/\phi(q_1)$. Since $d\leq q\leq u^{1/4}$,
$\rho_z(u/d)\ll\rho_z(u)$ uniformly in $z$.
We obtain $u_1\rho_z(u_1)/q_1\ll u\rho_z(u)/q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:ramare-mass}
With the notation above,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-mass}
 \int_0^1\sum_{j<J}
 \frac{\Delta_jM_j}{\log t_j}\rho_z(M_j)\,\d z
 \ll x.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Since $t_{j+1}/t_j=1+O(t_j^{-1/3})$, the left-hand side is
bounded by a constant times
\[
 x\int_0^1\int_T^{2y}\frac{\rho_z(x/t)}{t\log t}\,\d t\,\d z.
\]
For $u>T$, integration in $z$ gives
\[
 \int_0^1\rho_z(u)\,\d z
 \leq\min\left\{1,
   \frac1{\log\{\log(2u)/\log(2T)\}}\right\}
\]
whenever the second expression is defined with positive denominator.
For $T\leq t\leq\sqrt x$ we have $u=x/t\geq\sqrt x$;
the $z$-integral is $O(1/\log L)$, while
$\int_T^{\sqrt x}\d t/(t\log t)\ll\log L$.
For $\sqrt x\leq t\leq2y$ we use $\rho_z\leq1$ and
$\int_{\sqrt x}^{2y}\d t/(t\log t)=O(1)$.
Together these estimates prove \eqref{eq:ramare-mass}.
\end{proof}

\section{Multiplicative Fourier analysis and Gauss sums}\label{sec:gauss}

For every $j,z$ and every character $\chi\pmod q$ put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bj}
 B_{j,z}(\chi):=\sum_{r\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}
    A_{j,z}(r)\overline{\chi(r)}.
\end{equation}
Fourier inversion, the triangle inequality, and Parseval give, for
any selected character $\chi_{j,z}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-l1}
 \sum_{r\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}|A_{j,z}(r)|
 \leq |B_{j,z}(\chi_{j,z})|
   +\left(\sum_{\substack{\chi\pmod q\\\chi\ne\chi_{j,z}}}
                  |B_{j,z}(\chi)|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
The character may depend on both $j$ and $z$.

For $v\in\Z$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gauss-def}
 G_q(v,\chi):=\sum_{r\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}\chi(r)\e(vr/q).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bj-Gauss}
 B_{j,z}(\chi)=\sum_{m\leq M_j}F(m)w_z(m)G_q(am,\ov\chi).
\end{equation}
\rev{We record three Gauss-sum estimates that will also be used to obtain the sharp constants.}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:gauss-l2}
For every $v\in\Z$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-l2}
 \sum_{\chi\pmod q}|G_q(v,\chi)|^2=\phi(q)^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Expand the square and use orthogonality of characters on
$(\Z/q\Z)^\times$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:gauss-pointwise}
For every $v\in\Z$ and every character $\chi\pmod q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-pointwise}
 |G_q(v,\chi)|\leq\sqrt{q(v,q)}.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
\rev{By the Chinese remainder theorem, it is enough to consider} $q=p^a$.
If the local character has conductor $p^b$, $1\leq b\leq a$,
then $G_{p^a}(v,\chi)$ vanishes unless $v_p(v)=a-b$;
in the nonzero case its modulus equals
$p^{a-b}p^{b/2}=p^{a-b/2}$.
For the principal character the sum is $c_{p^a}(v)$, whose
prime-power formula gives the same pointwise bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:gauss-l1}
Uniformly in $\chi\pmod q$ and $(a,q)=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-l1}
 \sum_{v\bmod q}|G_q(av,\chi)|
 \leq\frac4{\sqrt6}\phi(q)\sqrt q.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
The sum factors over prime powers. For a local conductor $p^b$,
$1\leq b\leq a$, precisely $\phi(p^b)$ classes have nonzero
Gauss sum, each of modulus $p^{a-b/2}$.
The local $\ell^1$ sum is thus $\phi(p^a)p^{b/2}$,
which is at most $\phi(p^a)p^{a/2}$.
For the principal character the Ramanujan-sum formula gives local
norm $2\phi(p^a)$; relative to $\phi(p^a)p^{a/2}$ it has factor
$2/p^{a/2}$. Only $p^a=2,3$ enlarge the product, and their
factors are $2/\sqrt2$ and $2/\sqrt3$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exceptional Fourier coefficient}

\begin{prop}\label{prop:exceptional}
If $M_j\geq q^4$, then, uniformly for $0\leq z\leq1$ and
all $\chi\pmod q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exceptional-bound}
 |B_{j,z}(\chi)|\ll
 \frac{\phi(q)}{\sqrt q}\,M_j\rho_z(M_j).
\end{equation}
Consequently the total contribution of the selected coefficient
$|B_{j,z}(\chi_{j,z})|$ in \eqref{eq:ramare-master}, over the
blocks with $M_j\geq q^4$, is $O(x/\sqrt q)$.
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
Group \eqref{eq:Bj-Gauss} by $m\pmod q$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:shiu-weight} and \eqref{eq:gauss-l1} give
\[
 |B_{j,z}(\chi)|
 \ll\frac{M_j\rho_z(M_j)}q
         \sum_{v\bmod q}|G_q(av,\ov\chi)|
 \ll\frac{\phi(q)}{\sqrt q}M_j\rho_z(M_j).
\]
Insert this in \eqref{eq:ramare-master} and use
Lemma~\ref{lem:ramare-mass} to obtain the claimed total bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Applying the pretentious large sieve}

Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dq-Hq}
 \mathcal D_q:=\{d\geq1:p\mid d\Rightarrow p\mid q\},\qquad
 H(q):=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-1/2})^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Let $\eta=1-1/\sqrt2$ and define, for $M\geq q^4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mathfrakD}
 \mathfrak D(M,q):=
 \left(\frac{\log(q\log M)}{\log M}\right)^\eta
 \log\left(2+\frac{\log M}{\log(q\log M)}\right).
\end{equation}
We use the following direct specialization of
\cite[Theorem~1.9]{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019}.

\begin{lem}[Granville--Harper--Soundararajan]\label{lem:PLS}
Let $g\in\mathcal C(1)$ and $M\geq q^4$. There is a
character $\chi_0\pmod q$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PLS}
 \left(\sum_{\substack{\chi\pmod q\\\chi\ne\chi_0}}
   \left|\sum_{n\leq v}g(n)\chi(n)\right|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \ll v\mathfrak D(M,q)
\end{equation}
uniformly for $\sqrt M\leq v\leq M$.
If no exceptional character is needed, choose $\chi_0$ arbitrarily.
\end{lem}

\begin{prop}\label{prop:weighted-pls}
If $M_j\geq q^4$, then for each $z\in[0,1]$ there exists a character
$\chi_{j,z}\pmod q$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-pls}
 \left(\sum_{\substack{\chi\pmod q\\\chi\ne\chi_{j,z}}}
  |B_{j,z}(\chi)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \ll H(q)\bigl(\sqrt q\,M_j\mathfrak D(M_j,q)
     +\phi(q)M_j^{3/4}\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
Every $m$ has a unique factorization $m=dn$ with
$d\in\mathcal D_q$ and $(n,q)=1$. Since $q<T$, we have
$w_z(dn)=w_z(n)$. Define
\[
 g_z(n):=F(n)w_z(n)\mathbf1_{(n,q)=1}.
\]
It is multiplicative and belongs to $\mathcal C(1)$: for $p\nmid q$
and $p>T$ its local generating function equals
\[
 1+z\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{F(p)^k}{p^{ks}}
 =\frac{1-(1-z)F(p)p^{-s}}{1-F(p)p^{-s}},
\]
so that
$\Lambda_{g_z}(p^k)=F(p)^k\{1-(1-z)^k\}\log p$;
for $p\leq T$ (away from $q$) the usual bound holds, and for
$p\mid q$ the function is zero. Thus $|\Lambda_{g_z}(n)|\leq\Lambda(n)$.

For $(n,q)=1$, the change of variables in the Gauss sum gives
$G_q(adn,\ov\chi)=\chi(n)G_q(ad,\ov\chi)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bj-factor}
 B_{j,z}(\chi)=\sum_{\substack{d\leq M_j\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}
 F(d)G_q(ad,\ov\chi)
 \sum_{n\leq M_j/d}g_z(n)\chi(n).
\end{equation}
Choose $\chi_{j,z}$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:PLS} with $M=M_j$.
For $d\leq\sqrt{M_j}$, Minkowski's inequality, the pointwise
Gauss bound, and the large sieve give the contribution
\[
 \ll\sqrt q\,M_j\mathfrak D(M_j,q)
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{\sqrt{(d,q)}}d
 \leq H(q)\sqrt q\,M_j\mathfrak D(M_j,q).
\]
For $d>\sqrt{M_j}$, use the trivial inner-sum bound $M_j/d$.
\rev{Minkowski's inequality} and \eqref{eq:gauss-l2} give
\[
 \ll\phi(q)M_j
 \sum_{\substack{d>\sqrt{M_j}\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}\frac1d
 \leq H(q)\phi(q)M_j^{3/4}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:weighted-pls}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:short-M}
If $q\leq M_j<q^4$, then for every $z\in[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:short-M}
 \left(\sum_{\chi\pmod q}|B_{j,z}(\chi)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \leq \sqrt{2\phi(q)}\,M_j.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
Multiplicative Parseval and the enlargement to all additive
frequencies give
\[
 \sum_\chi|B_{j,z}(\chi)|^2
 \leq\phi(q)q\sum_{b\bmod q}
 \left|\sum_{\substack{m\leq M_j\\m\equiv b\pmod q}}
                   F(m)w_z(m)\right|^2.
\]
Each residue class contains at most $M_j/q+1$ integers;
$|F(m)w_z(m)|\leq1$ and $M_j\geq q$, so the last sum is at
most $2\phi(q)M_j^2$.
\end{proof}

\section{Summation of the Ramar\'e blocks}\label{sec:summing}

We combine \eqref{eq:ramare-master} with the preceding estimates.
Recall the standard bounds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-H-growth}
 \frac q{\phi(q)}\ll\log\log(3q),\qquad
 H(q)=\exp\left(O\left(\frac{\sqrt{\log(3q)}}
                                 {\log\log(3q)}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
In particular, for $q\leq8L^3$ the factors $q/\phi(q)$ and
$H(q)$ are $L^{o(1)}$.

For $M_j\geq q^4$, choose $\chi_{j,z}$ as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:weighted-pls}. By
\eqref{eq:fourier-l1}, Proposition~\ref{prop:exceptional}, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:ramare-mass}, the total contribution of the
exceptional coefficients is $O(x/\sqrt q)$.
The first term from \eqref{eq:weighted-pls} contributes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-I}
 \ll\frac{x}{\sqrt q}\frac q{\phi(q)}H(q)
 \int_T^{2x/q^4}\frac{\mathfrak D(x/t,q)}{t\log t}\,\d t.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the block mesh has relative width $O(t_j^{-1/3})$ and
allows comparison with the displayed integral, including at its last
block. Writing $u=\log(x/t)$, and recalling $\eta=1-1/\sqrt2$, we have
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_T^{2x/q^4}\frac{\mathfrak D(x/t,q)}{t\log t}\,\d t
 &\ll (\log L)^{\eta+1}
   \int_{4\log q-\log2}^{L-10\log L}
                  \frac{u^{-\eta}}{L-u}\,\d u\\
 &\ll L^{-\eta}(\log L)^{\eta+2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:ramare-I} is
$\ll(x/\sqrt q)L^{-\eta+o(1)}$.
The second term in \eqref{eq:weighted-pls} contributes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-tail}
 \ll H(q)x^{3/4}
 \int_T^{2x/q^4}\frac{\d t}{t^{3/4}\log t}
 \ll \frac{H(q)x}{q\log(2q)}
 \ll\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
\rev{An empty integration range contributes zero.}

For $q\leq M_j<q^4$ no exceptional character is required.
Using Lemma~\ref{lem:short-M}, \eqref{eq:fourier-l1}, and

\[

 \int_{x/q^4}^{2x/q}\frac{\d t}{t\log t}
 \ll\frac{x\log(2q)}{L\sqrt{\phi(q)}}

The remaining terms satisfy

\begin{prop}\label{prop:smooth-core}
Suppose that $q\leq8(\log x)^3$, $(a,q)=1$, and $F:\N\to\U$
is multiplicative and completely multiplicative at every prime
$p\nmid q$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smooth-core}
 \sum_{\substack{n\leq x\\P^+(n)\leq x/q}}
      F(n)\e(an/q)
 \ll\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
\end{prop}

in the one-character reduction. After separating the factors supported on primes dividing $q$, the argument is common to all multiplicative functions; only the

For $|\beta|\leq1/(qx)$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, put

\end{equation}

$\alpha=a/q+\beta$ with $|\beta|\leq1/(qx)$. Recall $\mathcal D_q$ and

\[

\]

\subsection{Gauss sums at primes dividing \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}}

Every positive integer has a unique factorization $n=dm$, where
$d\in\mathcal D_q$ and $(m,q)=1$. Since $(d,m)=1$, ordinary
multiplicativity gives $f(n)=f(d)f(m)$. Fourier inversion on
$(\Z/q\Z)^\times$ therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-primary-exact}
 S_f(X,a/q)
 =\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}
   \sum_{\substack{d\leq X\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}
   f(d)G_q(ad,\ov\chi)M_\chi(X/d).
\end{equation}
The following local estimate is the source of the leading constant.

\begin{lem}[Local Gauss-sum bounds]
\label{lem:general-primary-kernel}
Uniformly in $\chi\pmod q$ and $(a,q)=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-primary-kernel}
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{|G_q(ad,\ov\chi)|}{d}
 \leq\frac4{\sqrt6}\sqrt q.
\end{equation}
For each fixed $0<\rho<1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-primary-weighted-kernel}
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{|G_q(ad,\ov\chi)|}{d^{1-\rho}}
 \ll_\rho q^{1/2+o(1)}.
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative and $|f(n)|\leq1$, then, for
all real $t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-primary-kernel}
 \left|\sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}
 \frac{f(d)G_q(ad,\ov\chi)}{d^{1+it}}\right|
 \leq\sqrt q.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
\rev{We prove the estimates prime by prime.} Factor $q=\prod_{p^e\Vert q}p^e$ and let
$\chi_p$ denote the component of $\chi$ modulo $p^e$.
The Chinese remainder theorem gives a constant $\omega(a,\chi)$ of
modulus one for which
\begin{equation}\label{eq:primary-CRT-factor}
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{f(d)G_q(ad,\ov\chi)}{d^{1+it}}
 =\omega(a,\chi)
 \prod_{p^e\Vert q}\left(\sum_{v\geq0}
  \frac{f(p^v)\chi^{(p)}(p)^v}{p^{v(1+it)}}
  G_{p^e}(p^v,\ov{\chi_p})\right),
\end{equation}
where $\chi^{(p)}=\prod_{\substack{r^b\Vert q\\r\ne p}}\chi_r$;
thus $|\chi^{(p)}(p)|=1$. More explicitly, the CRT expression for
$G_q$ has local additive coefficient $ad(q/p^e)^{-1}$; its unit part
can be removed from the local Gauss sum and contributes precisely the
character factors displayed in \eqref{eq:primary-CRT-factor}.
\rev{The factorization also holds after taking absolute values.}

For a local character of conductor $p^j$ with $1\leq j\leq e$,
$G_{p^e}(p^v,\ov{\chi_p})$ vanishes unless $v=e-j$, in which case
its modulus is $p^{e-j/2}$. The corresponding local contribution
to \eqref{eq:general-primary-kernel} is $p^{j/2}\leq p^{e/2}$.
For a principal local character the relevant Ramanujan sums are
\[
 c_{p^e}(p^{e-1})=-p^{e-1},\qquad
 c_{p^e}(p^v)=\phi(p^e)\quad(v\geq e).
\]
Consequently the local absolute norm equals $2$.
Only the factors $p^e=2,3$ have $2>p^{e/2}$, and their relative
contributions multiply to $4/\sqrt6$.
This proves \eqref{eq:general-primary-kernel}. Replacing $d^{-1}$ by
$d^{-1+\rho}$ gives local norms $p^{j/2+\rho(e-j)}$ in the
nonprincipal case and $O_\rho(p^{\rho e})$ in the principal case.
Their product is $q^{1/2+o(1)}$, proving the weighted bound.

Suppose now that $f$ is completely multiplicative. Set
\[
 z_p=f(p)p^{-it}\chi^{(p)}(p),\qquad |z_p|\leq1.
\]
The local factor in \eqref{eq:primary-CRT-factor} is
$\sum_{v\geq0}z_p^v p^{-v}G_{p^e}(p^v,\ov{\chi_p})$.
For conductor $p^j$, $j\geq1$, this has modulus at most
$p^{j/2}|z_p|^{e-j}\leq p^{e/2}$.
For the principal character the complete geometric sum is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:principal-kernel-contraction}
 -z_p^{e-1}+\frac{(1-p^{-1})z_p^e}{1-z_p/p}
 =-z_p^{e-1}\frac{1-z_p}{1-z_p/p}.
\end{equation}
For $|z|\leq1$,
\[
 \frac{|1-z|}{|1-z/p|}\leq\frac{2p}{p+1}
 \leq\sqrt p\leq p^{e/2}.
\]
Thus every local factor is at most $p^{e/2}$; multiplying over
$p^e\Vert q$ proves \eqref{eq:complete-primary-kernel}.
The empty product for $q=1$ is understood as $1$.
\end{proof}

 \frac{|G_q(ad,\ov\chi)|}{d}

\end{equation}

\begin{abstract}
Let $f$ be a $1$-bounded multiplicative function, and suppose that

\section{Introduction}

Let \(
 \U:=\{z\in\C:|z|\leq1\}\) and  $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative functions.
Exponential sums with multiplicative coefficients have been studied
extensively and have many applications in analytic number theory. A foundational  result was established by
Montgomery and Vaughan \cite{MontgomeryVaughan1977}, who obtained strong
bounds for such sums in terms of rational approximation to $\alpha$. 
The subject has since been developed further in several directions; see,
for example,
\cite{GranvilleSoundararajan2007,Goldmakher2012,
BoberGoldmakherGranvilleKoukoulopoulos2018,
LamzouriMangerel2022,BretecheGranville2022,
GranvilleLamzouri2026}
and the references therein.



A folklore conjecture predicts that, for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, if
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, $(a,q)=1$, and
$q\leq x/(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, then\footnote{We will prove this conjecture in forthcoming work.}
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{n\leq x}f(n)\e(n\alpha)
 \ll \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation*}
In this paper, we are concerned with the logarithmically weighted analogue
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L-definition}
 L_f(x,\alpha):=\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}n\e(n\alpha).
\end{equation}
Besides its relation to the unweighted sums through partial summation,
this logarithmic variant also arises naturally for Dirichlet characters in
P\'olya's Fourier expansion for character sums. 
Granville and Lamzouri recently proved, among other results, that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GL-bound}
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|
 \ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}+\log q
\end{equation}
holds whenever $|\alpha-a/q|\le 1/(qx)$ with $(a,q)=1$ and $q\le x$.  Their examples show that the natural  size of the first term above should be $(\log x)/\sqrt q$, while an initial range $n\le q^2$ (say) can contribute to  the size $\log q$.  They formulated the
following two conjectures.

\begin{conjecture}[Granville--Lamzouri {\cite[(1.5)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}}]
\label{conj:GL}
Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, where $(a,q)=1$ and $1\leq q\leq x$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GL-conjecture}
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}+\log q.
\end{equation}
\end{conjecture}

For the more precise form, 
we write $A(x)\lesssim B(x)$ if
$|A(x)|\leq(1+o_x(1))B(x)$ as $x\to\infty$.

\begin{conjecture}[Granville--Lamzouri {\cite[(1.6)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}}]
\label{conj:GL-sharp}
Under the hypotheses of Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL}, if
$q\leq(\log x/\log\log x)^2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:GL-sharp-conjecture}
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|\lesssim
 \frac4{\sqrt6}\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
\end{conjecture}

On the major arcs $q\le (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, by adapting the
pretentious approach of Granville, Harper and
Soundararajan \cite{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019} to the logarithmically weighted setting, Granville and Lamzouri obtained
an asymptotic formula for $L_f(x,\alpha)$ in terms of some primitive
characters; see \cite[Theorem~1.6, Corollary~1.3]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}. As a consequence, they proved Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL-sharp} in the range
\(
 q\ll (\log x)^2\exp(-c\sqrt{\log\log x})
\)
for some constant $c>0$. 
Together with their general estimate \eqref{eq:GL-bound}, this leaves Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL} open only in the interval
\[
 (\log x)^2\exp(-c\sqrt{\log\log x})
 <q<
 \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^2\log\log\log x.
\]
Therefore for the proof of our result, it will  be convenient to restrict to the range
\[
 \log x\leq q\leq \log^2 x.
\]

Our main result is the following.

\begin{thm}\label{thm:main}
Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq 1/(qx)$, $(a,q)=1$, and $1\leq q\leq x$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 +O(\log q),
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then the constant $4/\sqrt{6}$ improves to $1$. Both constants are best possible in their respective classes.
\end{thm}


Theorem~\ref{thm:main} immediately implies Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL}. It
also gives the sharp form of Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL-sharp} whenever the
secondary term is negligible.

\begin{cor}\label{cor:GL-conjecture}
Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL} holds.
\end{cor}

\begin{cor}\label{cor:subcritical}
Let $f:\N\to\U$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leq1/(qx)$, $(a,q)=1$, and
$q=o((\log x)^2/(\log\log x)^2)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subcritical}
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then $4/\sqrt{6}$ improves to 1.
Both constants are best possible in their respective classes. %Moreover, the range $q=o((\log x/\log\log x)^2)$ is best possible in order of magnitude for retaining the coefficients $4/\sqrt6$ and 1 in each class.
\end{cor}

We can immediately show that Conjecture~\ref{conj:GL-sharp} cannot hold
 throughout the full range \(q\leq({\log x}/{(\log\log x)})^2
\)
with the same constant $4/\sqrt{6}$. 
Fix $0<c\leq1$ and take
\(
 q\sim
 c({\log x}/{(\log\log x)})^2,
  f\equiv1\) and \( \alpha=1/q.
\)
Then
\[
 L_f(x,\alpha)=\sum_{n\le x}\frac{e(n/q)}{n}
 =-\operatorname{Log}(1-\e(1/q))+O(q/x),
\]
where $\operatorname{Log}$ denotes the principal branch, and hence
\[
 |L_1(x,1/q)|
 =\log q+O(1)
 =\left(2\sqrt c+o(1)\right)\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\]
Thus the coefficient $4/\sqrt6$ fails  whenever
$c>2/3$, and the coefficient $1$   fails whenever $c>1/4$. 
Thus the range $q=o((\log x/\log\log x)^2)$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:subcritical} is
essentially best possible, in the sense that it cannot in general be
extended to the full  range
$q\asymp(\log x/\log\log x)^2$.

\subsection{Structure of the proof}

We first reduce both cases in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} to the range
$\log x\leq q\leq(\log x)^2$. For multiplicative functions, this follows
directly as noted above. Though Granville and Lamzouri also treat the
completely multiplicative case
\cite[Theorem~1.6 and Corollary~7.1]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}, to obtain the
sharp coefficient $1$ needed here, we need to combine their major arc asymptotic
formula with the corresponding local factors of the Euler product. We record this short
calculation in Section~\ref{sec:reductions}.

We now describe the main argument. Throughout this paper, let $y:=q^2$. Integers with at most
one prime factor exceeding $y$ give a lower order contribution; see Section \ref{sec:sparse}. For the
remaining integers we use a two-prime Ramar\'e identity (see Section \ref{sec:ramare-gauss}) to expose two
distinct large prime factors and write
\[
 n=dcpr,\qquad d\mid q^\infty,\qquad (cpr,q)=1,
\]
where $d\mid q^\infty$ means that all prime factors of $d$ divide $q$. %,  we say $d$ is the  $q$-part of $n$. 
Multiplicativity then separates the four factors. Fourier inversion on
$(\Z/q\Z)^\times$ transforms the additive phase into a character sum
involving the Gauss sum $G_q(\chi;d)$. The two marked prime variables are then estimated by a second moment over
Dirichlet characters, using the distribution of primes in reduced residue classes. The contribution of the factor $d$, which is supported on the
primes dividing $q$, is handled separately. %through the Gauss sums $G_q(\chi;d)$.

The $d$-sum involving the Gauss sums can be estimated prime by prime by the Chinese remainder theorem. For multiplicative functions $f$ we obtain
\[
 \Bigg|
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}\frac{f(d)G_q(\chi;d)}{d}
 \Bigg|
 \leq
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}\frac{|G_q(\chi;d)|}{d}
 \leq \frac4{\sqrt6}\sqrt q.
\]
At a prime power $p^e\Vert q$, the local factor is at most $p^{e/2}$  except when the local character $\chi \pmod{p^e}$ is principal and $p^e=2$ or $3$.
These two exceptional factors contribute $2/\sqrt2$ and $2/\sqrt3$,
respectively. This is where the constant $4/\sqrt6$ comes from.
For completely multiplicative $f$, using $f(p^v)=f(p)^v$, we get
\[
 \Bigg|
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}\frac{f(d)G_q(\chi;d)}d
 \Bigg|
 \leq\sqrt q.
\]
 Apart from this distinction, the rest of the argument is the same in the two cases.
 
Finally, %after estimating the two marked prime variables, 
the weights from the two-prime Ramar\'e identity recombine into the harmonic sum over integers coprime
to $q$, with no further loss in the constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$. We estimate the
contribution from integers with at least two large prime factors in Sections~\ref{sec:two-large}, and then complete the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} in Sections~\ref{sec:completion}.

We first replace $\alpha$ by $a/q$. Since

\end{equation}
Thus it is enough to work at the rational point $a/q$. %The case $q=1$ is immediate from the trivial harmonic bound.

For general multiplicative functions, the range $q<\log x$ is already
covered by \cite[Corollary~1.3]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}. %Indeed, the error term there is $o((\log x)/\sqrt q)$ uniformly in this range.

 \sum_{\substack{m\leq x\\(m,q)=1}}
 \frac{f(m)\overline{\chi(m)}}m
 \Bigg|
 \leq
 \sum_{\substack{m\leq x\\(m,q)=1}}\frac1m
 =\sum_{r\le x,r|q}\frac{\mu(r)}{r}\sum_{n\le x/r}\frac{1}{n}
 =
 \frac{\phi(q)}q\log x+O(\log^2 q).
\]
Thus, using $|\tau(\chi)|=\sqrt\ell$, it remains to show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-local-bound}
 \frac{\sqrt\ell}{q}|\kappa(q/\ell)|
 \prod_{\substack{p\mid q\\p\nmid\ell}}
 \Bigg|1-\frac{f(p)\overline{\chi(p)}}p\Bigg|^{-1}
 \leq \frac1{\sqrt q}.%\Longleftrightarrow
\end{equation}

We verify this prime by prime. Write $p^e\Vert q$ and $p^j\Vert\ell$,
where $0\leq j\leq e$. If $j\geq1$, then $\chi(p)=0$ and
$\kappa(p^{e-j})=f(p)^{e-j}$. Hence the corresponding local factor on
the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:complete-local-bound} is at most
$p^{j/2-e}\leq p^{-e/2}$.
If $j=0$, put $z:=f(p)\overline{\chi(p)}$. Since $f=\kappa*\chi$ and
$f$ is completely multiplicative, we have
\[
 \kappa(p^e)=f(p)^e-\chi(p)f(p)^{e-1}\implies |\kappa(p^e)|=|f(p)^{e-1}||1-z|\le|1-z|.
\]
The corresponding local factor on
the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:complete-local-bound} is therefore at most
\[
 \frac1{p^e}\frac{|1-z|}{|1-z/p|}\le p^{-e+1/2}\le p^{-e/2},
\]
where we used $|1-z|\leq\sqrt p |1-z/p|$, since $|z|\leq1$ and 
\(
 p|1-z/p|^2-|1-z|^2
 =(p-1)\left(1-{|z|^2}/{p}\right)\geq0.
\)
Multiplying over the local factor at $p^e\Vert q$ proves
\eqref{eq:complete-local-bound}.

Substituting \eqref{eq:complete-local-bound}  into \eqref{eq:GL-complete} we get
\[
 |L_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leq (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\]
The two $O(\log^2 q)$ errors above contribute, after substitution into
\eqref{eq:GL-complete}, at most
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \log^2 q\left(
 \frac{\sqrt{\ell}}{\phi(q)}|\kappa(q/\ell)|
 +\frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \right)
 &\ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \bigl(2^{\omega(q)}+1\bigr)\log^2 q=
 o\left(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second term follows from \eqref{eq:complete-local-bound} and the first term comes from
\(
 |\kappa(a)|
\le
 2^{\omega(a)}.
\)
This proves the lemma.
\end{proof}



At the other end, if $q>(\log x)^2$, then \eqref{eq:GL-bound} and the
standard estimate $q/\phi(q)\ll\log\log(3q)$ give us
\(
 {\log x}/{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}\ll\log q.
\)
Thus both assertions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} follow in this range.

For the rest of the proof we may therefore assume
\( \log x\leq q\leq(\log x)^2.
\)
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:direct-facts}
 \log q\asymp\log\log x,
 \qquad
 \frac q{\phi(q)}\ll\log\log\log x.
\end{equation}
The integers now divisible by $p^2$ for some prime $p>y$
have total harmonic weight
\[
 \ll(\log x)\sum_{p>y}\frac1{p^2}
 \ll\frac{\log x}{y}
 =o\left(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\right).
\]
After deleting them, let $L_0$, $L_1$, and $L_{\geq2}$ denote the
parts of $L_f(x,a/q)$ for which $\omega_y(n)$ is respectively $0$, $1$,
and at least $2$. Thus we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decomposition}
 L_f(x,a/q)
 =
 L_0+L_1+L_{\geq2}
 +o\left(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{equation}

\section{Integers with at most one large prime factor}\label{sec:sparse}

We show that the contribution from integers with at most one prime
factor exceeding $y=q^2$ is negligible. %The $y$-smooth part follows directly from Mertens' theorem. For the terms with one large prime factor, we write $n=pm$ and split according to whether $m\leq\sqrt q$ or $m>\sqrt q$.

\begin{prop}\label{prop:sparse}
In the range $\log x\leq q\leq(\log x)^2$, we have
\[
 |L_0|+|L_1|
 \ll
 \log\log x
 +o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg).
\]
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
The contribution of $L_0$ is immediate from Mertens' theorem:
\[
 |L_0|=\bigg|
 \sum_{\substack{n\leq x\\P^+(n)\leq y}}
 \frac{f(n)}n\e(an/q)
 \bigg|
 \leq
 \prod_{p\leq y}\bigg(1-\frac1p\bigg)^{-1}
 \ll\log y
 \ll\log\log x.
\]

We now turn to $L_1$. After removing the terms divisible by $p^2$ for
some $p>y$, as in the previous section, every remaining integer counted
by $L_1$ can be written uniquely as $n=pm$, where $p>y$ and
$P^+(m)\leq y$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L1-formula}
 L_1
 =
 \sum_{p>y}\frac{f(p)}p
 \sum_{\substack{m\leq x/p\\P^+(m)\leq y}}
 \frac{f(m)}m\e(amp/q).
\end{equation}

We first consider $m\leq\sqrt q$. We may replace $p\leq x/m$ by  $p\leq x/\sqrt q$, at a cost
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{m\leq\sqrt q}\frac1m
 \sum_{x/\sqrt q<p\leq x/m}\frac1p
 &\ll
 \log q\bigg(-\log\big(1-\frac{\log q}{2\log x}\big) +O\big(\frac1{\log x}\big) \bigg) \ll
 \frac{\log^2 q}{\log x}
 =o(1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $\sqrt q<y$, the condition $P^+(m)\leq y$ is automatic. 
Thus, after grouping the prime variable by its residue class modulo $q$,
the contribution from $m\leq\sqrt q$ is
\[
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times} A(u)V(u)
 \ll \|A\|_2\|V\|_2,
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz, where
\[
 A(u):=
 \sum_{\substack{y<p\leq x/\sqrt q\\p\equiv u\pmod q}}
 \frac{f(p)}p,
 \qquad
 V(u):=
 \sum_{m\leq\sqrt q}\frac{f(m)}m\e(amu/q).
\]

For $\|A\|_2$, let $I=(P,2P]$ be a dyadic interval.  We write $$A(u)=\sum_I A_I(u),\quad A_I(u):=
\sum_{\substack{p\in I\\ p\equiv u\pmod q}}\frac{f(p)}p.$$ 
Since
$P\geq y=q^2$, $\log (P/q)\asymp\log P$, then by the Brun--Titchmarsh inequality and partial summation formula, we get
\[
 \max_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}|A_I(u)|\le \max_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}
 \sum_{\substack{p\in I\\p\equiv u\pmod q}}\frac1p
 \ll
 \frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{p\in I}\frac1p.
\]
Hence by Minkowski's inequality, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|A\|_2
 &\leq \sum_I\|A_I\|_2
 \leq
 \sum_I
 \bigg(
 \max_u|A_I(u)|
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}|A_I(u)|
 \bigg)^{1/2}\\
 &\leq
 \sum_I
 \bigg(
 \frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \bigg)^{1/2}
 \ll
 \frac1{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}
 \sum_I\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \ll
 \frac{\log\log x}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For $\|V\|_2$, let $c_q(h):= \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}\e(hu/q)$ denote the Ramanujan sum. For $m\neq n$, the standard bound $|c_q(h)|\le(q,h)$ gives
$|c_q(m-n)|\le(q,m-n)\le |m-n|<\sqrt q. $ Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|V\|_2^2
 &=
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}|V(u)|^2
 =
 \sum_{m,n\leq\sqrt q}
 \frac{f(m)\overline{f(n)}}{mn}\,c_q(m-n)\\
 &\ll
 \phi(q)\sum_{m\leq\sqrt q}\frac1{m^2}
 +
 \sqrt q\sum_{\substack{m,n\leq\sqrt q\\m\neq n}}\frac1{mn}\ll
 \phi(q)+\sqrt q \log^2 q
 \ll \phi(q).
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this with the bound for $\|A\|_2$, the contribution from
$m\leq\sqrt q$ is \( \|A\|_2\|V\|_2\ll\log\log x.
\)

We now consider $m>\sqrt q$. Split the prime variable into dyadic
intervals $I=(P,2P]$. For $p\in I$, we replace $m\leq x/p$ by  $\sqrt q<m\leq x/(2P)$. The omitted boundary terms are
bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_I\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \sum_{x/(2P)<m\leq x/p}\frac1m
 &\ll
 \sum_I\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \ll \log\log x.
\end{aligned}
\]

For a fixed $I$, grouping both variables by their residue classes
modulo $q$, the contribution from the interval $I$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigg|
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times} &A_I(u)\sum_{v\bmod q}
C_I(v)\e(auv/q) \bigg|
\le 
\|A_I\|_2 \Bigg(\sum_{u\bmod q}
\bigg|
\sum_{v\bmod q}C_I(v)\e(auv/q)
\bigg|^2\Bigg)^{1/2}\\
 &\le
 \|A_I\|_2 \Bigg(\sum_{v,w\bmod q}
C_I(v)\overline{C_I(w)}
\sum_{u\bmod q}\e(au(v-w)/q)\Bigg)^{1/2}
\le
 \sqrt q\,\|A_I\|_2\|C_I\|_2
 \end{aligned}
\]
where 
\[
C_I(v):=
 \sum_{\substack{\sqrt q<m\leq x/(2P)\\
                  P^+(m)\leq y\\
                  m\equiv v\pmod q}}
 \frac{f(m)}m,
\]
and
$$ \begin{aligned} \|C_I\|_2^2 &\leq \max_{v\bmod q}|C_I(v)| \sum_{v\bmod q}|C_I(v)|
\ll
\frac{\log x}{q}  \sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\P^+(m)\leq y}}\frac1m\ll  \frac{\log x\log\log x}{q}. \end{aligned} $$

Now, summing over the dyadic intervals $I$ and using the same estimate for $\|A_I\|_2$ as above, we obtain the contribution from $m>\sqrt{q}$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sqrt q\sum_I\|A_I\|_2\|C_I\|_2
 &\ll
 \sqrt q\sum_I
 \frac1{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}
 \bigg(\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\bigg)
 \bigg(\frac{\log x\log\log x}{q}\bigg)^{1/2}\\
 &\ll
 (\log\log x)^{3/2}
 \sqrt{\frac{\log x}{\phi(q)}}
 =
 o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg),
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used
\(
 \sum_I\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\ll\log\log x
\)
and \eqref{eq:direct-facts}. Together with the boundary terms and the
range $m\leq\sqrt q$, this proves the proposition.
\end{proof}



\section{The Ramar\'e decomposition and Gauss sums}
\label{sec:ramare-gauss}

We now turn to $L_{\geq2}$.  A standard use of Ramar\'e's identity is to
extract one prime factor from an integer and thereby obtain a bilinear
decomposition.
The usual form (see, for example, \cite[Section~17.3]{FriedlanderIwaniec2010} and
\cite{MatomakiRadziwill2016}) is
\[
 \mathbf 1_{\omega_{\mathcal P}(n)\geq1}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{p\mid n\\p\in\mathcal P}}
 \frac1{\omega_{\mathcal P}(n)}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{pm=n\\p\in\mathcal P}}
 \frac1{\omega_{\mathcal P}(m)+\mathbf 1_{p\nmid m}},
\]
where  \( \omega_{\mathcal P}(n):=\#\{p\in\mathcal P:p\mid n\}
\) for some set of primes $ \mathcal P$.
For our purpose it is more convenient to extract two distinct primes
$p,r>y$ at the same time. This leaves two prime variables for the
character second moment used below.

We therefore use a slight reformulation of Ramar\'e's identity. The
elementary identity
\[
 \frac1{k(k-1)}
 =
 \int_0^1(1-t)t^{k-2}\,dt
 \qquad (k\geq2)
\]
replaces the combinatorial weight by the multiplicative weight
$t^{\omega_{\mathcal P}(\,\cdot\,)}$. This gives the following
two-prime form.

\begin{lem}[Two-prime Ramar\'e identity]\label{lem:ramare}
Suppose that no prime $p>y$ satisfies $p^2\mid n$ and that
$\omega_y(n)\geq2$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare}
 1=
 \int_0^1(1-t)
 \sum_{\substack{p,r>y,\ p\neq r\\pr\mid n}}
 t^{\omega_y(n/(pr))}\,\d t.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
This follows directly from the identity we stated above by writting $k:=\omega_y(n)$.
\end{proof}


For each marked pair $p,r$, write
\[
 d:=\prod_{\ell\mid q}\ell^{v_\ell(n)},
 \qquad
 c:=\frac{n}{dpr}.
\]
Thus $d$ is the part of $n$ supported on the primes dividing $q$.
Since $p,r>y>q$, we have $(d,cpr)=(c,pr)=(p,r)=1$ and $(c,q)=1$.
Multiplicativity therefore gives $f(n)=f(d)f(c)f(p)f(r)$. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:ramare}, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramare-decomposition}
\begin{aligned}
 L_{\geq2}
 ={}&\int_0^1(1-t)
 \sum_{\substack{c\geq1,\ (c,q)=1\\
                  v_\ell(c)\leq1\ (\ell>y)}}
 \frac{f(c)t^{\omega_y(c)}}c
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}\frac{f(d)}d 
 \sum_{\substack{p,r>y,\ p\neq r\\
                  p\nmid c,\ r\nmid c\\dcpr\leq x}}
 \frac{f(p)f(r)}{pr}\e(adcpr/q)\,\d t.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

We now expand the additive character in Dirichlet characters modulo $q$.
For $\chi\pmod q$ and $n\in\Z$, write
\[
 \tau(\chi,n):=
 \sum_{u\bmod q}\chi(u)\e(nu/q)
\]
where $\tau(\chi,1)=\tau(\chi)$ is the Gauss sum, and if $(n,q)=1$, then
\(
 \tau(\chi,n)=\overline{\chi(n)}\,\tau(\chi).
\)
If $(m,q)=1$, then  by the orthogonality on $(\Z/q\Z)^\times$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:character-expansion}
 \e(adm/q)
 =
 \frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{\chi\bmod q}
 \tau(\overline{\chi},ad)\chi(m).
\end{equation}

\begin{lem}\label{lem:gauss}
For every $\chi\pmod q$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gauss-l1}
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{d}
 \leq
 \frac4{\sqrt6}\sqrt q.
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gauss-complete}
 \bigg|
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}
 \frac{f(d)\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)}{d}
 \bigg|
 \leq
 \sqrt q.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $X\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gauss-tail}
 \sum_{\substack{d>X\\d\mid q^\infty}}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{d}
 \ll_\varepsilon
 \frac{q^{1/2+\varepsilon}}{\sqrt X}.
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
By the Chinese remainder theorem, it is enough to estimate the
corresponding sums prime by prime. Let $q=p^e$, and suppose that $\chi$
is induced by a primitive character $\chi^\ast\pmod{p^j}$, where
$0\leq j\leq e$. If $j\geq1$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \tau(\overline{\chi},ap^v)
 &=
 \begin{cases}
  0, & v\neq e-j,\\[2mm]
  p^{e-j}\chi^\ast(a)\tau(\overline{\chi^\ast}),
  & v=e-j,
 \end{cases}\\
 \sum_{v\geq0}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ap^v)|}{p^v}
 &=
 \frac{p^{e-j}|\tau(\overline{\chi^\ast})|}{p^{e-j}}
 =
 p^{j/2}
 \leq p^{e/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here we used the standard formula
$|\tau(\chi^\ast)|=p^{j/2}$ for primitive characters.

If $j=0$, then $\chi$ is principal modulo $p^e$, and
$\tau(\overline{\chi},ap^v)=c_{p^e}(ap^v)$. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{v\geq0}\frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ap^v)|}{p^v}
 &=
 \frac{p^{e-1}}{p^{e-1}}
 +\phi(p^e)\sum_{v\geq e}\frac1{p^v}
 =2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Returning to general $q$, we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}\frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{d}
 &\leq
 \sqrt q
 \prod_{\substack{p^e\Vert q\\
                   \chi\pmod{p^e}\ {\rm principal}}}
 \max\bigg(1,\frac2{p^{e/2}}\bigg)
 \leq
 \sqrt q\,\frac2{\sqrt2}\frac2{\sqrt3}
 =
 \frac4{\sqrt6}\sqrt q.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:Gauss-l1}.

Suppose now that $f$ is completely multiplicative. By the Chinese
remainder theorem, the sum in \eqref{eq:Gauss-complete} factors prime
by prime, up to unit factors of modulus $1$. For $p^e\Vert q$, the
nonprincipal case contributes at most $p^{j/2}\leq p^{e/2}$. In the
principal case, after absorbing the unit factor into $f(p)$, the local
sum contributes, for some $|z|\le1$,
\[
 \bigg|z^{e-1}\frac{z-1}{1-z/p}\bigg|
 \leq\frac{|1-z|}{|1-z/p|}
 \leq\sqrt p
 \leq p^{e/2},
\]
by the same inequality $|1-z|\leq\sqrt p |1-z/p|$ we used in Lemma~\ref{lem:complete-small-q}.
Multiplying over $p^e\Vert q$ proves \eqref{eq:Gauss-complete}.

Finally,  we use Rankin's trick to bound
\[
 \sum_{\substack{d>X\\d\mid q^\infty}}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{d}
 \leq
 X^{-1/2}
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{\sqrt d}.
\]
The same calculation at prime power $p^e$ gives
\[
 \sum_{v\geq0}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ap^v)|}{p^{v/2}}
 \leq
 p^{e/2}\bigg(1+\frac2{\sqrt p}\bigg),
\]
and therefore \eqref{eq:Gauss-tail} follows by
\[
 \sum_{d\mid q^\infty}
 \frac{|\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)|}{\sqrt d}
 \ll
 \sqrt q\prod_{p\mid q}\bigg(1+\frac2{\sqrt p}\bigg)
 \ll_\varepsilon \sqrt q\,q^\varepsilon.
\]
\end{proof}


\section{Integers with at least two large prime factors}
\label{sec:two-large}

We now estimate $L_{\geq2}$. If one uses the Brun--Titchmarsh inequality
throughout, it is easy to obtain
\(
 L_{\geq2}\ll {(\log x)}/{\sqrt q}.
\)
However, to get the sharp constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$, we have to  make extra effort. 
Remember that the integer $n$ in this section is understood to satisfy
\(
 \omega_y(n)\geq2\) and \( p^2\nmid n \quad \text{for every prime } p>y.\) We will sometime omit these conditions.

\begin{prop}\label{prop:two-large}
In the range $\log x\leq q\leq(\log x)^2$, we have
\[
 |L_{\geq2}|
 \leq
 \bigg(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\bigg)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}+O(1).
\]
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then
\[
 |L_{\geq2}|
 \leq
 (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}+O(1).
\]
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Split the prime variables into dyadic intervals
$I=(P,2P]$ and $J=(R,2R]$, we define
\[
  X:=\frac{x}{4cPR},\quad
P_{\chi,c}(I):=
 \sum_{\substack{p\in I\\p\nmid c}}
 \frac{f(p)\chi(p)}p \quad \text{and}
 \quad
 D_\chi(X):=
 \sum_{\substack{d\leq X\\d\mid q^\infty}}
 \frac{f(d)\tau(\overline{\chi},ad)}d.
\]
The choice of $X$ separates the condition $dcpr\leq x$ on each dyadic
block. %Indeed, if $d\leq X$, then for $p\in I$ and $r\in J$, we have \(  dcpr  \leq  \frac{x}{4cPR}\,c(2P)(2R)  =x. \)

If $d>X$, then
\(
 {x}/{4}<n=dcpr\leq x.
\)
After summing over $c,I,J$, taking absolute values and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:ramare}, the total
contribution of all such terms to $L_{\ge2}$ is at most
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\int_0^1(1-t)
 \sum_{\substack{x/4<n\leq x}}%\\ omega_y(n)\geq2}}
 \frac1n
 \sum_{\substack{p,r>y,\ p\neq r\\pr\mid n}}
 t^{\omega_y(n/(pr))}\,\d t
 \leq
 \sum_{x/4<n\leq x}\frac1n
 \ll1.
\end{aligned}
\]


For $d\leq X$, we have $dcpr\leq x$ for every
$p\in I$ and $r\in J$. After temporarily including the diagonal \(p=r\) when \(I=J\), whose contribution is acceptable, we have, by plugging
\eqref{eq:character-expansion} into \ref{eq:ramare-decomposition},

\begin{align}
 L_{\geq2}
 =&
 \int_0^1(1-t)
 \sum_{\substack{c\geq1,\ (c,q)=1\\
                  v_\ell(c)\leq1\;(\ell>y)}}
 \frac{f(c)t^{\omega_y(c)}}{c\phi(q)}
 \sum_{I,J}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}
 \chi(c)D_\chi(X)
 P_{\chi,c}(I)P_{\chi,c}(J)\d t
 +O(1)+o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg)\notag\\
 ={}&
 \int_0^1 (1-t) \sum_{\substack{c\geq1,\ (c,q)=1\\
                  v_\ell(c)\leq1\;(\ell>y)}}t^{\omega_y(c)}
 \sum_{I,J}
 L_{\geq2,\mathrm{block}}(c;I,J)\,\d t
 +O(1) +o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg),\label{eq:block}
\end{align}
where
\[
 L_{\geq2,\mathrm{block}}(c;I,J)
 :=
 \frac{f(c)}{c\phi(q)}
 \sum_{\chi\bmod q}
 \chi(c)D_\chi(X)
 P_{\chi,c}(I)P_{\chi,c}(J).
\]
By character orthogonality and the same Brun--Titchmarsh estimate used
in Section~\ref{sec:sparse},
\begin{align}\label{eq:prime-sec}
 \sum_{\chi\bmod q}|P_{\chi,c}(I)|^2
 &=
 \phi(q)
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}
 \bigg|
 \sum_{\substack{p\in I,\ p\nmid c\\p\equiv u\pmod q}}
 \frac{f(p)}p
 \bigg|^2
 \ll
 \bigg(\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\bigg)^2.
\end{align}
Then by \eqref{eq:Gauss-l1}, \eqref{eq:prime-sec}, and Cauchy--Schwarz, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BT-block}
 |L_{\geq2,\mathrm{block}}(c;I,J)|
 \le
\frac{1}{c\phi(q)}
\max_{\chi}|D_\chi(X)|
\sum_{\chi\bmod q}
|P_{\chi,c}(I)P_{\chi,c}(J)|
 \ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{c\phi(q)}
 \bigg(\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\bigg)
 \bigg(\sum_{r\in J}\frac1r\bigg).
\end{equation}

We now fix $0<\delta<1$ and put \( z:=\exp((\log x)^\delta).\)
We first consider the part of $L_{\geq2}$ for which at least one of the two marked
primes lies between $y$ and $z$.
 By \eqref{eq:BT-block} and \eqref{eq:block}, and extending the sums, their total contribution is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq z}\frac1p\bigg)
 \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac1p\bigg)
 \int_0^1(1-t)\sum_{\substack{c\leq x,\ (c,q)=1\\
                  v_\ell(c)\leq1\;(\ell>y)}}
 \frac{t^{\omega_y(c)}}c\,\d t
 +O(1)\\
 &\ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq z}\frac1p\bigg)
 \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac1p\bigg)
 \frac{\phi(q)}q\log x
 \int_0^1(1-t)
 \exp\bigg(-(1-t)\sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac1p\bigg)\,\d t
 +O(1)\\
 &\ll
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq z}\frac{1}{p}\bigg)
      \bigg(\sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac{1}{p}\bigg)^{-1}
 +O(1)\\
 &\ll
 \frac{\delta+o(1)}{1+o(1)}
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 +O(1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{\substack{c\leq x,\ (c,q)=1\\
                  v_\ell(c)\leq1\;(\ell>y)}}
 \frac{t^{\omega_y(c)}}c\leq
 \prod_{\substack{p\leq y\\p\nmid q}}
 \bigg(1-\frac1p\bigg)^{-1}
 \prod_{y<p\leq x}\bigg(1+\frac tp\bigg)\\
 & =
 \prod_{\substack{p\leq x\\p\nmid q}}
 \bigg(1-\frac1p\bigg)^{-1}
 \prod_{y<p\leq x}
 \bigg(1-\frac1p\bigg)\bigg(1+\frac tp\bigg)
 \ll
 \frac{\phi(q)}q\log x\,
 \exp\bigg(-(1-t)\sum_{y<p\leq x}\frac1p\bigg).
\end{aligned}
\]


It remains to consider the part of $L_{\geq2}$ for which both marked
primes exceed $z$. Since $p\in(P,2P]$ and
$r\in(R,2R]$, we have $P,R\geq z/2$. Since \( q\leq(\log x)^2\leq(\log P)^{2/\delta},
\) we can apply the Siegel--Walfisz theorem to get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prime-second-sharp}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{\chi\bmod q}|P_{\chi,c}(I)|^2
 &=
 \phi(q)
 \sum_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}
 \bigg|
 \sum_{\substack{p\in I,\ p\nmid c\\p\equiv u\pmod q}}
 \frac{f(p)}p
 \bigg|^2\\
 &\leq
 \phi(q)
 \max_{u\in(\Z/q\Z)^\times}
 \sum_{\substack{p\in I\\p\equiv u\pmod q}}\frac1p
 \sum_{p\in I}\frac1p
 \leq
 \bigl(1+o(1)\bigr)
 \bigg(\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\bigg)^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Suppose $X=x/(4cPR)<\log x$, then \( \frac{x}{4\log x}<cpr\leq x.\)
Using \eqref{eq:BT-block} and Lemma~\ref{lem:ramare}, the total
contribution of these blocks is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{x/(4\log x)<m\leq x}\frac1m\ll
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}\log\log x
 =
 o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg),
\end{aligned}
\]
by \eqref{eq:direct-facts}, which is negligible.

We are left with $X\geq\log x$. For a general multiplicative function,
\eqref{eq:Gauss-l1} gives
\[
 |D_\chi(X)|
 \leq
 \frac4{\sqrt6}\sqrt q.
\]
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, then
\eqref{eq:Gauss-complete} and \eqref{eq:Gauss-tail} give, for $\varepsilon=1/8$ (say),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |D_\chi(X)|
 &\leq
 \sqrt q+ O_\varepsilon\bigg(\frac{q^{1/2+\varepsilon}}{\sqrt X}\bigg)
 =
 (1+o_x(1))\sqrt q.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence, by \eqref{eq:prime-second-sharp} and Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |L_{\geq2,\mathrm{block}}(c;I,J)|
 &\leq
 \frac{\max_\chi|D_\chi(X)|}{c\phi(q)}
 \bigg(\sum_{\chi\bmod q}|P_{\chi,c}(I)|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
 \bigg(\sum_{\chi\bmod q}|P_{\chi,c}(J)|^2\bigg)^{1/2}\\
 &\leq
 \bigg(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o_x(1)\bigg)
 \frac{\sqrt q}{c\phi(q)}
 \bigg(\sum_{p\in I}\frac1p\bigg)
 \bigg(\sum_{r\in J}\frac1r\bigg)
\end{aligned}
\]
in the multiplicative case. If $f$ is completely multiplicative, the same
estimate holds with $4/\sqrt6$ replaced by $1$.

To recombine the prime sums, we may drop the conditions $p\nmid c$ and
$r\nmid c$. %Together with the diagonal $p=r$ introduced above, the additional terms contain the square of a prime exceeding $y$. 
The corresponding loss is
\[
 \ll
 (\log x)(1+\log\log x)
 \sum_{p>y}\frac1{p^2}
 =
 o\bigg((\log x)\frac{\phi(q)}q\bigg),
\]
which is again negligible  to $L_{\geq2}$.
For the remaining terms, put $m=cpr$ and write
\[
 K:=\omega_y(m),
 \qquad
 K_z:=\#\{p>z:p\mid m\}.
\]
For each fixed $m$, the marked primes can be chosen in
$K_z(K_z-1)$ ordered ways, while the two-prime Ramar\'e weight gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K_z(K_z-1)
 \int_0^1(1-t)t^{K-2}\,\d t
 &=
 \frac{K_z(K_z-1)}{K(K-1)}
 \leq1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, in the multiplicative case, the contribution from $p,r>z$ and
$X\geq\log x$ is at most
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\bigg(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o_x(1)\bigg)
 \frac{\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{\substack{m\leq x\\(m,q)=1}}\frac1m
 =
 \bigg(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o_x(1)\bigg)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 +o\bigg(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}\bigg).
\end{aligned}
\]
For completely multiplicative $f$, the same argument gives
\(
 (1+o_x(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\)

Combining this with the contribution from the range in which at least
one marked prime lies in $(y,z]$, we obtain
\[
 |L_{\geq2}|
 \leq
 \bigg(
 \frac4{\sqrt6}+O(\delta)+o_x(1)
 \bigg)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 +O(1)
\]
for general multiplicative functions, and $4/\sqrt{6}$ replaced by 1 for completely multiplicative functions. We finally let $x\to\infty$ first
with $\delta$ fixed, and then let $\delta\to0$. This proves the
proposition.
\end{proof}



\section{Completion of the proof}\label{sec:completion}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
From \eqref{eq:decomposition},
Proposition~\ref{prop:sparse}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:two-large}, we get
\[
 |L_f(x,a/q)|
 \leq
 \bigg(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\bigg)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
 +O(\log\log x).
\]
Since $\log\log x\ll\log q$ in this range, this proves
\eqref{eq:main} at $a/q$, and \eqref{eq:phase-error} returns us to
$\alpha$.
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, the second part of
Proposition~\ref{prop:two-large} gives us the same result with $4/\sqrt{6}$ replaced by 1.

The constant $4/\sqrt6$ is best possible by
\cite[Example~1.7]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}. To see that the constant $1$
is also best possible, we fix a primitive character $\chi\pmod{q_0}$ and
take $f=\overline{\chi}$ and $\alpha=a/q_0$, where $(a,q_0)=1$. Then
\[
 L_f(x,a/q_0)
 =
 \frac{\chi(a)\tau(\overline{\chi})}{q_0}\log x+O(1) \implies
 |L_f(x,a/q_0)|
 =
 (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{q_0}}.
\]
\end{proof}
